prompt: What is a data contract?
hint: It is between two teams.

choices.text: A licence that lets the data team copy the app’s database
choices.why: Permission to copy is access control; the contract is about what the data means and how it changes.

choices.text: A written agreement on the fields and how changes are announced
choices.why: Right: producer and reader agree on fields, meaning, types and notice.

choices.text: A schema the database enforces so a column is never renamed
choices.why: A contract does not freeze the source; the app still has to evolve.

choices.text: The invoice a provider sends for storing the data
choices.why: That is a bill, which is the cost row of the table, not the contract row.

prompt: Under a contract, the app team announces two weeks ahead that `start_station` will be renamed. What has the contract changed?
hint: Compare it with the rename in lesson 1.

choices.text: The rename is blocked until the data team agrees to it
choices.why: The contract gives notice, not a veto over how the app evolves.

choices.text: The pipeline now reads columns by position rather than by name
choices.why: Reading by position breaks on a reorder instead; it is not what the contract does.

choices.text: A surprise became a date that the pipeline could be ready for
choices.why: Right: the pipeline is ready on the day of the rename.

choices.text: Nothing, since a rename breaks a pipeline whatever was agreed
choices.why: With notice, the pipeline is changed first and does not break.

prompt: Which law governs the personal data Roda Livre keeps about its customers in Brazil?

choices.text: The LGPD, enforced by the ANPD
choices.why: Right: the Lei Geral de Proteção de Dados, enforced by the ANPD.

choices.text: No law, as long as the data stays inside the company
choices.why: Keeping it in-house does not take it out of the law; holding it is processing it.

choices.text: The terms of use the customer accepted in the app
choices.why: Terms of use sit beneath the law and cannot set it aside.

choices.text: The GDPR, because the data lives in the cloud
choices.why: The GDPR is the European regulation; Brazilian customers fall under the LGPD.

prompt: Which of these are among what a data engineer at Roda Livre is answerable for? Choose all that apply.
hint: Seven were listed.

choices.text: How fresh the rides are at 09:00
choices.why: Yes: freshness is one of the seven.

choices.text: The price of a ride
choices.why: That is a business decision; the engineer delivers the data it is judged by.

choices.text: A description of what each table means
choices.why: Yes: documentation is one of the seven.

choices.text: The monthly bill for storage and queries
choices.why: Yes: cost is one of the seven.

choices.text: Which stations the van visits first
choices.why: That is Marta’s call, made with the data the engineer delivers.

prompt: What do Reis and Housley mean by the undercurrents?
hint: Where in the lifecycle do they appear?

choices.text: Phases done after the pipeline is built, such as securing it
choices.why: That is the picture the section corrects: a stage that skipped them hands the gap on.

choices.text: Questions asked at every stage, from generation to delivery
choices.why: Right: each is a question asked at every stage.

choices.text: The storage and compute that sit beneath a warehouse
choices.why: Those are layers of a product; the undercurrents are concerns of the work.

choices.text: Costs that do not show on the provider’s bill
choices.why: Hidden costs are real, but they are what-it-costs, not this list.

prompt: Match each undercurrent to the question it asks at every stage.
hint: Read the question each one asks.

pairs.right: who can read and change this?
what does it mean, and who owns it?
what runs when, and in what order?
is it versioned, reviewed and tested?

prompt: The first copy of the rides keeps each customer’s phone number. Why is removing it later expensive?
hint: Follow the number downstream.

choices.text: Phone numbers are stored encrypted and cannot be deleted
choices.why: Encryption does not stop deletion; the trouble is how many places hold it.

choices.text: Every table, report and person downstream of it gets the number
choices.why: Right: fixing it at the end means finding every copy.

choices.text: The LGPD forbids changing data once it has been collected
choices.why: The law asks for the opposite: data kept no longer than its purpose needs.

choices.text: Orchestration has to be rebuilt for each change
choices.why: A schedule does not hold data; the copies do.

prompt: Caio asks for read access to the payments table to try a new model. Which undercurrent’s question should be answered first?
hint: Payments are readable by two people today.

choices.text: Orchestration
choices.why: Nothing has to run on a schedule yet; this is about who may read.

choices.text: Software engineering
choices.why: Version control matters for code; the request is for access to data.

choices.text: Security
choices.why: Right: who can read this, and is it the fewest people who need to?

choices.text: DataOps
choices.why: Automation and monitoring come after deciding whether he may read it.

prompt: Why does the list of six skills name no particular warehouse or scheduler?
hint: What is each of those products?

choices.text: Because those products are taught in this course instead
choices.why: This course names them; other courses teach them.

choices.text: Each one is a product doing one of the six jobs in its own way
choices.why: Right: learnt after the six, a product takes weeks.

choices.text: Because employers have stopped asking for them in adverts
choices.why: Adverts are full of them; the section says they rest on the six.

choices.text: Because they change too fast to be worth learning
choices.why: They are worth learning, one at a time, on top of the six.

prompt: Marta asked for a live map of bicycles per station. What did ana’s question about its use reveal?
hint: Ask what she will do with it.

choices.text: That the map had to update every second to be useful
choices.why: The van leaves twice a day; seconds buy nothing.

choices.text: A picture before each van run
choices.why: Right: a batch job twice a day, with data an hour or two old.

choices.text: That the request was curiosity and could wait a year
choices.why: The van driver acts on it every day; it is not curiosity.

choices.text: That Marta needed a stream of dock readings, as asked
choices.why: That was the literal request, and the most expensive reading of it.

prompt: The finance manager asks ana for "real-time revenue". Which question should she ask first?
hint: Before any tool.

choices.text: Which stream processor would the finance team like us to use?
choices.why: That chooses a tool before anybody knows the need.

choices.text: Should the data be stored as Parquet or as Avro files?
choices.why: A format question, asked before the problem is known.

choices.text: How many dashboards does the finance team want?
choices.why: A count of screens says nothing about how fresh the data must be.

choices.text: What will you do differently with it?
choices.why: Right: the answer decides what "real time" has to mean.

prompt: What is an SLI?
hint: I is for indicator.

choices.text: A target the team sets for itself
choices.why: That is the objective, the SLO.

choices.text: A measurement, such as the data’s age at 09:00
choices.why: Right: the indicator is what is measured.

choices.text: A promise to a customer, with a penalty
choices.why: That is the agreement, the SLA.

choices.text: A log of the incidents of the month
choices.why: A log records failures; the indicator measures every morning, good or bad.

prompt: Why is Roda Livre’s two-hour objective tighter than the four-hour agreement with the city?
hint: Who hears first?

choices.text: Because the city checks the data twice as often as Marta does
choices.why: The difference is not about who checks more; it is about who hears first.

choices.text: Because objectives and agreements are measured in different units
choices.why: Both are hours of age; the same measurement sits under both.

choices.text: So the team hears of trouble first
choices.why: Right: a breach of the objective leaves time to fix it before the promise breaks.

choices.text: To pay a smaller discount
choices.why: The discount follows the agreement; the objective carries no money.

prompt: `freshness.py` reports `repairs.csv` as BREACH at 63.5 hours on a Monday. What should change?
hint: When do the mechanics save the sheet?

choices.text: The mechanics should save their sheet every hour
choices.why: Nobody reading repairs needs hourly data; the feed is fine.

choices.text: The objective for that feed
choices.why: Right: each feed gets an objective set by what its readers need.

choices.text: The program, because `os.utime` set the wrong time
choices.why: The listing shows 17:30 on Friday, the time that was intended.

choices.text: The clock, because Friday was recorded in another time zone
choices.why: Every time in the program carries the São Paulo zone.

prompt: In the freshness check, how many hours old was `payments.csv` at 09:00?
hint: It last landed at 06:50.

prompt: In the September simulation, on how many of the thirty mornings were the rides fresh?
hint: The SLI line of the output.

prompt: An objective says fresh on 95% of mornings, measured over a 30-morning month. How many bad mornings can the month have and still meet it?
hint: Work out 5% of 30.

choices.text: Two
choices.why: Two leaves 28 of 30, which is 93.3%: September missed with exactly two.

choices.text: One
choices.why: Right: 5% of 30 is one and a half, so in practice one.

choices.text: Zero
choices.why: That would be a 100% objective; 95% leaves some room.

choices.text: Five
choices.why: Five of thirty is about 17%, far past 5%.

prompt: Besides freshness, which indicator covers most of what readers of a table care about?
hint: Did it all arrive?

choices.text: Completeness, whether every row of the day arrived
choices.why: Right: yesterday’s rides counted against the count the source reports.

choices.text: The number of people who read it each week
choices.why: Popularity says nothing about whether the data is whole.

choices.text: The size of the file on disk
choices.why: A file can be large and still miss a day of rides.

choices.text: How long the load took to run last night
choices.why: Speed of a load is not whether everything arrived.

prompt: In SLO, the O stands for ___.
hint: The target the team sets itself.

prompt: What is a two-way door, in the sense of Amazon’s 2015 letter?
hint: You can walk back through it.

choices.text: A decision you undo at modest cost if it was wrong
choices.why: Right: make it quickly, close to where it matters.

choices.text: A decision two teams have to approve before it is made
choices.why: Approval is about who decides, not about whether it can be undone.

choices.text: A system that both reads data and writes it
choices.why: The doors are kinds of decision, not kinds of system.

choices.text: A choice that deserves weeks of careful thought
choices.why: That describes the one-way door.

prompt: Which of these Roda Livre decisions is a one-way door?
hint: Which one leaves nothing to go back to?

choices.text: Moving the dashboards to another tool next quarter
choices.why: A week of rebuilding charts, and it can be done again.

choices.text: Renaming a column with two weeks’ notice
choices.why: A rename with notice can be renamed back.

choices.text: Deleting raw files after 30 days
choices.why: Right: once they are gone, no question about that period can be answered.

choices.text: Trying a new chart library on one report
choices.why: One report on a trial is the model two-way door.

prompt: Which of these lowers lock-in?
hint: What lets the engine change while the data stays?

choices.text: Writing every query in the provider’s own dialect of SQL
choices.why: Every function only one product has is a line to rewrite on leaving.

choices.text: Signing a longer contract for a lower monthly price
choices.why: A longer contract raises the cost of leaving.

choices.text: Keeping raw data in an open format that many engines read
choices.why: Right: Parquet can be read by dozens of engines.

choices.text: Choosing whichever provider the biggest companies use
choices.why: Popularity makes a tool mature, not easy to leave.

prompt: Which statement about managed and self-hosted is the section’s?
hint: What does each one cost?

choices.text: Self-hosted is cheaper in general, since there is no charge per use
choices.why: The hours are the missing cost, and for a team of two they are the scarcer thing.

choices.text: Managed means the provider owns the data from then on
choices.why: The provider runs the software; the data stays yours.

choices.text: They differ in who runs the software, and that is all
choices.why: Who runs it changes the bill, the hours and the control.

choices.text: Neither is cheaper in general
choices.why: Right: managed trades hours for a bill, and the balance depends on the team.

prompt: A new database is at version 0.4, and searching its error messages finds nothing. Which criterion does this speak to?
hint: Who has already hit the problems?

choices.text: Lock-in
choices.why: Leaving it could be easy; the worry is running it.

choices.text: Total cost
choices.why: Nothing here is about money yet.

choices.text: Maturity
choices.why: Right: a small population has met its problems before you.

choices.text: Reversibility
choices.why: Reversibility is about the decision, not about how proven the tool is.

prompt: With the weights for a team of two, what total did "PostgreSQL we run" get?
hint: The first ranking.

prompt: Between the two rankings `matrix.py` prints, the winner changes. What changed?
hint: Compare the two dictionaries printed.

choices.text: The scores Davi gave each option on each criterion
choices.why: SCORES is the same for both rankings.

choices.text: The weights, the priority given to each criterion
choices.why: Right: the same scores under other priorities give another winner.

choices.text: The list of options being compared
choices.why: The same three options appear in both.

choices.text: The criteria the options are scored on
choices.why: The five criteria are printed, identical, in both.

prompt: Raising one score by one point made the managed warehouse win, 38 to 36. What does that say about the first result?
hint: Compare one point with the uncertainty of a score.

choices.text: That Caio’s scoring is more accurate than Davi’s
choices.why: Neither is shown to be more accurate; both are judgements.

choices.text: That the matrix was built with a mistake
choices.why: The arithmetic is right; the margin is small.

choices.text: That the managed warehouse is the better choice after all
choices.why: One nudged cell does not make a winner either.

choices.text: The two are equivalent on these criteria
choices.why: Right: the choice goes to something the matrix does not hold.

prompt: A colleague who already prefers one option adjusts the numbers until it comes out top. What is this?
hint: When were the scores written?

choices.text: Counting one thing twice
choices.why: That is criteria that overlap, such as two kinds of cost.

choices.text: Résumé-driven development
choices.why: That is about why a tool is wanted, not how a matrix is filled.

choices.text: Scoring after deciding
choices.why: Right: the matrix launders a preference into a calculation.

choices.text: Weighting for growth
choices.why: Choosing weights openly is the method; bending scores to an answer is not.

prompt: In McKinley’s sense, what makes a technology boring?
hint: Think of its failures.

choices.text: It is old and slow, and chosen by habit
choices.why: That is the picture the section replaces.

choices.text: Its failures are already known
choices.why: Right: a failure with a name, a search result and a fix.

choices.text: It has stopped releasing new versions
choices.why: Boring tools keep being released; what matters is that they are well understood.

choices.text: Nobody puts it on a CV
choices.why: CVs are about the chooser; boring is about the tool’s known failures.

prompt: Where should Roda Livre spend an innovation token, if it spends one?
hint: What does the company compete on?

choices.text: On a novel database for storing rides
choices.why: Storing rides well is not what wins customers.

choices.text: On a new scheduler for the nightly copies
choices.why: A schedule is plumbing; it should be boring.

choices.text: On the forecast of which stations will run dry before the van
choices.why: Right: that is close to having a bicycle where somebody wants one.

choices.text: On a stream processor for Marta’s van report
choices.why: The van report needs data twice a day, not a stream.

prompt: Which of these is evidence for leaving a boring tool?
hint: Measured or predicted?

choices.text: A forecast that it will not scale next year
choices.why: A forecast is the weaker kind of evidence the section warns about.

choices.text: A conference talk about a faster tool
choices.why: A talk is about somebody else’s problem.

choices.text: A job advert that asks for a newer tool
choices.why: That is the pull of résumé-driven development.

choices.text: A query Marta needs that took ten minutes this morning
choices.why: Right: a measured fact, and a token is better spent on one.

prompt: Put the parts of Davi and ana’s decision record in the order they appear.
hint: From the title to the last line.
items: a numbered title stating the decision
trap: The facts come before the decision they led to.

prompt: The team later moves its tables to a managed warehouse. What happens to ADR 3?
hint: An accepted record is not edited.

choices.text: It is edited to describe the new decision
choices.why: Editing it erases the reasoning that was true at the time.

choices.text: It is deleted, since it no longer applies
choices.why: Deleting it loses the history the record exists to keep.

choices.text: A new record supersedes it
choices.why: Right: ADR 3 is marked superseded and stays readable.

choices.text: A comment is added to the code that reads the tables
choices.why: A comment in code is not where the reasoning is looked for.

prompt: Which "revisit when" condition is the most useful to write?
hint: Which one can a person check?

choices.text: When the team feels the database has become slow
choices.why: A feeling arrives late and argues; a measurement does not.

choices.text: When a query Marta needs passes a minute
choices.why: Right: a measurement, so the question comes back by itself.

choices.text: When a better database appears on the market
choices.why: Better tools appear every month; this would reopen it forever.

choices.text: Some day, when there is time for it
choices.why: That is the "revisit some day" the line exists to replace.

prompt: Which part of an ADR ages, and is the reason to keep it?
hint: Facts true at the time.

choices.text: The context of the decision
choices.why: Right: a later reader can check whether those facts still hold.

choices.text: The number in the title
choices.why: The number is an identifier; it does not age.

choices.text: The list of people who decided
choices.why: Names say who to ask; they are not what a reader judges.

choices.text: The status line at the top of the record
choices.why: Status changes when a record is superseded; it is not the facts.

prompt: How many gigabytes is a year of dock readings, according to `cost.py`?
hint: The first line of the output.

prompt: What made the first managed plan cost 1226.12 a month in queries?
hint: Same engine, same price, as the second plan.

choices.text: A higher price per terabyte than the second plan
choices.why: Both plans use the same invented price.

choices.text: Re-reading a whole year of readings every five minutes
choices.why: Right: how the engine is used moved the bill, not the tool.

choices.text: Keeping a full year of readings in storage
choices.why: Storage was 0.71 a month in every plan.

choices.text: The two hours of an engineer each month
choices.why: Those are the people line, 240.00, not queries.

prompt: "Our own server" has no charge per query, yet it is the most expensive plan. Why?
hint: Look at the people column.

choices.text: The server’s hourly price is the highest price in the program
choices.why: The server line is 432.00; the people line is larger.

choices.text: It stores the readings twice
choices.why: Storage is the same 0.71 in every plan.

choices.text: Ten hours of upkeep a month, at an engineer’s price
choices.why: Right: 1200.00 of people, the largest line in any plan.

choices.text: It reads the whole year on every refresh
choices.why: That is the first managed plan; this one charges nothing per read.

prompt: Deleting raw files to save on storage: what would it save at Roda Livre, by the program’s prices?
hint: A year of readings cost 0.71 a month to keep.

choices.text: About twelve hundred reais a month
choices.why: That was the queries of the five-minute plan, not storage.

choices.text: Less than one real a month
choices.why: Right: and the door it walks through is one-way.

choices.text: The cost of the server, 432.00 a month
choices.why: The server runs whether the files exist or not.

choices.text: Two hours of an engineer each month
choices.why: Deleting files does not remove the upkeep.

prompt: Match each term to what it is.
hint: Five terms from this lesson.

pairs.right: the target the team sets itself
a promise outside, with a consequence

prompt: Which of these belong to the total cost of a technology? Choose all that apply.
hint: Three terms.

choices.text: The provider’s bill
choices.why: Yes: the first term, and the only one on an invoice.

choices.text: The hours of the people who run it
choices.why: Yes: the largest line in two of the three plans.

choices.text: Its place in a survey of popular tools
choices.why: Popularity bears on maturity, not on cost.

choices.text: What it would cost to leave it
choices.why: Yes: paid once and late, which is why it is left out.

choices.text: The number of features it advertises
choices.why: Features are a reason to want it; they are not a cost.

prompt: A decision that cannot be undone is a ___-way door.
hint: The opposite of two-way.

prompt: A company with twenty engineers pays a large monthly bill for a managed warehouse and has spare hours on the team. How does the section’s reasoning apply?
hint: Which resource is scarce here?

choices.text: Managed is cheaper whatever the size of the team
choices.why: The section says neither is cheaper in general.

choices.text: With hours spare and a large bill, self-hosting is worth pricing
choices.why: Right: with hours to spare and a big bill, the balance tips the other way.

choices.text: Lock-in rules out any change, so the question is closed
choices.why: Lock-in is a price to know, not a wall.

choices.text: The team should add a third option to the matrix and let its total decide
choices.why: A matrix shows where people disagree; its total does not decide.

prompt: Marta’s van report gets a new objective: at most one hour old at 09:00. Which part of the September run would you expect to change, and why?
hint: On 3 September the data was an hour and twenty minutes old.

choices.text: Nothing, since the objective is a target and not a measurement
choices.why: The measurement stays; how many mornings pass it changes.

choices.text: The ages themselves, which would come out smaller
choices.why: A target does not move the data; it moves the line.

choices.text: Three breaches instead of two
choices.why: Right: 3 September’s 1h20 now crosses the line as well.

choices.text: The agreement with the city, which has to tighten with it
choices.why: The agreement is a separate promise; the team tightens its own target alone.
